title: Generative Modeling: VAEs, GANs & Diffusion
description: Autoregressive models, Variational Autoencoders (ELBO, Reparameterization Trick), GANs (Minimax, WGAN), and Latent Diffusion (DDPM).

sections.title: Generative Modeling Foundations
sections.subtitle: Learning the Underlying Data Distribution $p(x)$ to Synthesize High-Fidelity Novel Artifacts

sections.title: Discriminative vs Generative Modeling
sections.text:
- **Discriminative Models:** Model the conditional probability $P(Y \mid X)$, learning a decision boundary to separate classes.
- **Generative Models:** Model the joint distribution $P(X, Y)$ or data distribution $P(X)$. They must understand the entire underlying structure of the data manifold to generate realistic new samples $x_{new} \sim P_{model}(X)$.

sections.title: The Four Modern Generative Paradigms
rows: Autoregressive Models
Factorizes joint distribution into product of conditionals: $P(X) = \prod_{t=1}^T P(x_t \mid x_{<t})$.
Slow (sequential $O(T)$ steps).
Exceptional density estimation; no mode collapse.
Large Language Models (GPT-4), Audio generation.
Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)
Maximizes Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) via encoder $q_\phi(z|x)$ and decoder $p_\theta(x|z)$.
Instant ($1$ forward pass).
Smooth latent space; tends to produce blurry images due to MSE/Gaussian assumptions.
Latent space representation, compression, drug molecule design.
Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)
Two-player minimax game between Generator $G(z)$ and Discriminator $D(x)$: $\min_G \max_D V(D, G)$.
Instant ($1$ forward pass).
Sharp, photo-realistic details; highly vulnerable to training instability and **Mode Collapse**.
Real-time face generation (StyleGAN), image editing.
Diffusion Models (DDPM / Score-Based)
Gradually corrupts data with Gaussian noise (Forward), then trains a network to invert the noise step-by-step (Reverse).
Historically slow (requires 20-50 denoising steps), but fast with modern ODE solvers.
State-of-the-art fidelity, zero mode collapse, stable training objective.
Image synthesis (Stable Diffusion, Midjourney, DALL-E 3), video generation (Sora).

sections.title: VAE: The Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) & Reparameterization Trick
sections.text:
True marginal likelihood $\log p_\theta(x)$ is intractable. VAE maximizes the **ELBO**:

$$\log p_\theta(x) \ge \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z|x)}[\log p_\theta(x|z)] - D_{KL}(q_\phi(z|x) \parallel p(z))$$

- **Reconstruction Term:** $\mathbb{E}[\log p_\theta(x|z)]$ forces decoder to accurately reconstruct inputs.
- **Regularization Term:** $D_{KL}$ pulls the posterior $q_\phi(z|x)$ toward a standard Gaussian prior $\mathcal{N}(0, I)$, ensuring a continuous, interpolatable latent manifold.

> **The Reparameterization Trick:** Sampling $z \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ is stochastic and non-differentiable. By setting $z = \mu + \sigma \odot \epsilon$ where $\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$, gradients flow smoothly into $\mu$ and $\sigma$ via standard backpropagation!

sections.title: Latent Diffusion & Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG)
sections.body:
Running diffusion directly on high-resolution pixels ($1024 \times 1024$) is computationally ruinous. **Latent Diffusion Models (LDM / Stable Diffusion)** solve this by compressing images into a lower-dimensional latent space using a pretrained VAE, performing the iterative denoising diffusion process entirely in latent space.

**Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG, Ho & Salimans, 2022):** Balances sample quality and prompt adherence without an auxiliary classifier:

$$\tilde{\epsilon}_\theta(z_t, c) = \epsilon_\theta(z_t, \emptyset) + s \cdot (\epsilon_\theta(z_t, c) - \epsilon_\theta(z_t, \emptyset))$$

Where $s > 1$ (typically $7.0 - 9.0$) boosts conditioning signal $c$, creating sharp images aligned with the prompt.

code_example.title: Variational Autoencoder (VAE) Latent Space & Reparameterization in NumPy
code_example.code:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Simulated VAE Encoder and Reparameterization Trick
def reparameterize(mu, logvar):
    std = np.exp(0.5 * logvar)
    eps = np.random.randn(*mu.shape) # Gaussian noise epsilon ~ N(0, I)
    return mu + std * eps

def kl_divergence(mu, logvar):
    # KL divergence between N(mu, var) and standard normal N(0, I)
    return -0.5 * np.sum(1 + logvar - np.square(mu) - np.exp(logvar), axis=-1)

# 4 samples with simulated mu and logvar in 2D latent space
np.random.seed(42)
mu = np.array([[2.0, 1.0], [-1.5, 0.5], [0.1, -2.0], [1.2, -1.0]])
logvar = np.array([[-0.2, 0.1], [0.0, -0.5], [0.2, 0.2], [-0.1, -0.1]])

z_samples = reparameterize(mu, logvar)
kl_losses = kl_divergence(mu, logvar)

print('Mean vector mu:\n', mu)
print('Sampled Latent Vectors z (differentiable):\n', np.round(z_samples, 3))
print('KL Divergence per sample:', np.round(kl_losses, 4))

# Visualize latent points
plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4))
plt.scatter(mu[:, 0], mu[:, 1], color='red', s=100, label='Mean Centers (mu)')
plt.scatter(z_samples[:, 0], z_samples[:, 1], color='blue', s=80, marker='x', label='Stochastic z Samples')
plt.title('VAE Reparameterization: Latent Embedding Manifold')
plt.xlabel('z_1'); plt.ylabel('z_2'); plt.grid(True); plt.legend()
plt.show()

quiz.question: What is the fundamental objective difference between discriminative and generative models?
options: Discriminative models estimate P(Y | X) to separate classes; generative models estimate the underlying distribution P(X) to generate new samples
Discriminative models run faster
Generative models can only output binary values
They are identical mathematically
quiz.explanation: Discriminative algorithms learn class boundaries; generative models capture the full distribution to generate novel realistic data.

quiz.question: What are the two components of the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) in Variational Autoencoders?
options: Reconstruction Likelihood and the KL Divergence from the approximate posterior to the prior
Cross-entropy loss and L1 regularization
Generator loss and Discriminator loss
Mean squared error and learning rate
quiz.explanation: ELBO balances reconstruction quality (how well the decoder recreates input x) with KL divergence (pulling the latent distribution toward a standard normal Gaussian).

quiz.question: What is the Reparameterization Trick in VAEs (Kingma & Welling, 2013)?
options: Expressing latent vector z as z = mu + sigma * epsilon where epsilon ~ N(0, I), allowing backpropagation through mu and sigma
Using a lookup table for random numbers
Replacing gradients with integers
Quantizing the latent vector to 8 bits
quiz.explanation: Direct sampling z ~ N(mu, sigma) has no derivative; expressing z deterministically in terms of mu and sigma with an external random variable epsilon allows backprop.

quiz.question: Why do standard VAEs often generate slightly blurry images compared to GANs?
options: Because standard VAEs optimize pixel-wise Mean Squared Error (MSE), which represents an average of plausible high-frequency textures rather than sharp edges
Because VAEs cannot use convolutional layers
Because VAEs have too many parameters
Because latent space has negative dimensions
quiz.explanation: Pixel-level L2 reconstruction loss penalizes high-frequency mismatches heavily, encouraging the model to hedge bets by predicting blurry pixel averages.

quiz.question: What is the two-player minimax objective of a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN, Goodfellow et al., 2014)?
options: min_G max_D [ E_{x}[log D(x)] + E_{z}[log(1 - D(G(z)))] ]
min_G min_D [ (G(z) - x)^2 ]
max_G max_D [ log D(x) + log G(z) ]
min_G [ D(x) + G(z) ]
quiz.explanation: The discriminator D maximizes its accuracy in classifying real vs fake samples; the generator G minimizes the probability that D detects its generated fakes.

quiz.question: What is 'Mode Collapse' in Generative Adversarial Networks?
options: When the generator discovers a small handful of realistic samples that successfully fool the discriminator and produces only those few outputs, losing all dataset diversity
When the GPU runs out of VRAM
When the loss evaluates to negative infinity
When the generator produces black images only
quiz.explanation: Mode collapse occurs when the generator collapses onto a single narrow mode of the distribution (e.g. generating only one specific dog face repeatedly).

quiz.question: What is the 'Vanishing Gradient' pathology in standard minimax GAN training?
options: When the discriminator becomes too strong early on, causing D(G(z)) -> 0, which makes the gradient log(1 - D(G(z))) with respect to G saturate to zero
When the discriminator weights decay to zero
When the learning rate becomes zero
When images are too bright
quiz.explanation: If the discriminator learns too quickly, its classification is virtually perfect, leaving the generator with zero gradient to learn from.

quiz.question: What is the Non-Saturating GAN heuristic proposed by Goodfellow to fix vanishing gradients?
options: Training G to maximize log(D(G(z))) instead of minimizing log(1 - D(G(z)))
Setting discriminator learning rate to zero
Inverting the discriminator weights
Normalizing pixel values between -1 and 1
quiz.explanation: Maximizing log(D(G(z))) provides large gradients early when D easily rejects fakes, preventing generator training stagnation.

quiz.question: What is the Wasserstein GAN (WGAN, Arjovsky et al., 2017)?
options: A GAN variant that optimizes the Earth Mover's (Wasserstein-1) Distance, providing smooth, continuous gradients everywhere even with disjoint support distributions
A GAN developed in Germany
A GAN for generating water images
A model using quadratic programming
quiz.explanation: WGAN replaces the Jensen-Shannon divergence with the Wasserstein distance, eliminating mode collapse and providing an interpretable loss curve.

quiz.question: What theoretical condition must the Critic function satisfy in Wasserstein GAN?
options: It must be a 1-Lipschitz continuous function: ||f(x) - f(y)|| <= ||x - y||
It must output probabilities between 0 and 1
It must have zero bias
It must be an orthogonal matrix
quiz.explanation: By the Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality, the Wasserstein distance formulation requires the critic to be a 1-Lipschitz continuous function.

quiz.question: How did the original WGAN enforce the Lipschitz condition, and why was it flawed?
options: By weight clipping to [-c, c], which caused parameters to concentrate at extremes and led to capacity underutilization and gradient vanishing/exploding
By using ReLU
By dividing weights by 10
By using L1 regularization
quiz.explanation: Weight clipping naively bounds gradients, forcing weights to polarize at the thresholds [-c, c] and severely impairing representational capacity.

quiz.question: How does WGAN with Gradient Penalty (WGAN-GP, Gulrajani et al., 2017) enforce the Lipschitz condition?
options: By penalizing the norm of the critic's gradient with respect to interpolated inputs: (||grad_{x_hat} D(x_hat)||_2 - 1)^2
By clipping gradients to 1.0
By setting learning rate to 0.0001
By using batch normalization
quiz.explanation: WGAN-GP penalizes deviations of the critic's gradient norm from 1 along straight lines between real and generated samples.

quiz.question: What architectural innovation did StyleGAN (Karras et al., NVIDIA 2019) introduce?
options: Mapping noise z through a mapping network into an intermediate style space w, which modulates convolutional feature maps via Adaptive Instance Normalization (AdaIN)
Using 100 discriminator networks
Replacing convolutions with fully connected layers
Using transformers exclusively
quiz.explanation: StyleGAN maps z to disentangled style space w and injects styles at each convolution resolution via AdaIN, enabling fine-grained scale-specific attribute control.

quiz.question: What are Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM, Sohl-Dickstein 2015, Ho et al. 2020)?
options: Generative models that systematically add Gaussian noise in a forward process, and train a neural network to predict and remove noise step-by-step in a reverse process
Models that simulate chemical gas diffusion
Random walk models for stock prices
Networks that diffuse heat across GPUs
quiz.explanation: DDPMs formulate generation as a reverse Markov chain that iteratively denoises pure Gaussian noise into realistic data samples.

quiz.question: What does the neural network (typically a U-Net or DiT) predict in a standard DDPM?
options: The added Gaussian noise vector epsilon_t present in the noisy image x_t at time step t
The final clean image directly in 1 step
The class label of the noise
The total number of time steps
quiz.explanation: Predicting the noise vector epsilon_t proves mathematically and empirically superior to predicting the clean image x_0 directly.

quiz.question: What is the forward (noising) process in DDPM?
options: A fixed, non-learned Markov chain that adds Gaussian noise with variance schedule beta_t at each step: q(x_t | x_{t-1}) = N(x_t; sqrt(1 - beta_t) * x_{t-1}, beta_t * I)
A network trained with backpropagation
A method for blurring images with Photoshop
A downsampling operation
quiz.explanation: The forward process is an analytical diffusion process that steadily destroys data structure until x_T becomes isotropic Gaussian noise.

quiz.question: Can you sample noisy image x_t at arbitrary time step t directly in closed form without iterating through all previous steps?
options: Yes, using the formula x_t = sqrt(alpha_bar_t) * x_0 + sqrt(1 - alpha_bar_t) * epsilon where alpha_bar_t is the cumulative product of (1 - beta_i)
No, you must step through every step sequentially
Only if t is an even number
Only on GPUs
quiz.explanation: The Gaussian property allows closed-form sampling of x_t directly from x_0 at any arbitrary time step t in O(1) time.

quiz.question: What is the loss function used to train DDPM models?
options: Simple Mean Squared Error between the actual injected Gaussian noise and the noise predicted by the U-Net: ||epsilon - epsilon_theta(x_t, t)||^2
Adversarial minimax loss
Binary Cross-Entropy
Contrastive InfoNCE loss
quiz.explanation: Ho et al. showed that unweighted MSE between true noise and predicted noise yields state-of-the-art sample quality.

quiz.question: Why is the standard DDPM sampling process slow at inference time?
options: Because generating an image requires evaluating the heavy neural network sequentially across hundreds or thousands of iterative denoising steps (e.g. 1000 steps)
Because GPUs cannot run diffusion
Because images must be uploaded to the cloud
Because noise cannot be calculated in parallel
quiz.explanation: Generating a sample requires rolling back the reverse Markov chain step-by-step, taking 500-1000 sequential forward passes per image.

quiz.question: What is DDIM (Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models, Song et al., 2020)?
options: A non-Markovian deterministic sampling formulation that allows generating high-quality samples in 20-50 steps instead of 1000 steps
A 1-bit diffusion model
A model that diffuses audio
A method for training without GPUs
quiz.explanation: DDIM formulates the reverse process as a deterministic ordinary differential equation (ODE), dramatically accelerating sampling by 20x-50x.

quiz.question: What is Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG, Ho & Salimans, 2022)?
options: A technique that conditions generation on text prompts while periodically dropping the prompt during training (e.g. 10%), interpolating between conditional and unconditional predictions
Using an external ResNet classifier to filter bad images
A method for generating text without an LLM
A model that runs without a loss function
quiz.explanation: CFG trains a single model for both conditional and unconditional generation, amplifying the conditioning vector to significantly improve prompt alignment.

quiz.question: What is the effect of setting the Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) scale too high (e.g. s = 25)?
options: The generated image suffers from oversaturation, unnatural contrast, high-frequency artifacts, and burnt color degradation
The image becomes completely black
The image resolution doubles
The generation finishes in 1 second
quiz.explanation: Excessive guidance pushes latent vectors outside the training manifold, resulting in over-saturated, hyper-contrasted, distorted artifacts.

quiz.question: What is Latent Diffusion (Rombach et al., CVPR 2022 / Stable Diffusion)?
options: Training diffusion models in the compressed latent space of a pretrained autoencoder (VAE) rather than raw pixel space, reducing computational cost by 95%
Diffusing images across multiple servers
A model that generates hidden text
A diffusion model that runs on CPUs only
quiz.explanation: By operating in a perceptually equivalent 8x-downscaled latent space (e.g. 64x64 latent for a 512x512 image), Latent Diffusion drastically slashes training and inference FLOPs.

quiz.question: What is the U-Net architecture in diffusion models?
options: An encoder-decoder network with skip connections that downsamples feature maps and then upsamples them, preserving fine spatial details across scales
A network shaped like the letter V
A single-layer recurrent network
A network without any convolutions
quiz.explanation: The U-Net architecture uses contraction, bottleneck, and expansion paths with lateral skip connections, ideal for predicting spatial noise residuals.

quiz.question: What is a Diffusion Transformer (DiT, Peebles & Xie, 2023)?
options: Replacing the standard U-Net backbone in diffusion models with a pure Vision Transformer operating on latent patches, powering modern models like Sora and Flux
A model that translates text into French
A transformer that diffuses memory across GPUs
A recurrent model for audio
quiz.explanation: DiT demonstrated that Transformers scale predictably with compute in diffusion tasks, outperforming U-Nets as model capacity increases.

quiz.question: What is Flow Matching (Lipman et al., 2023)?
options: A generative modeling framework based on Continuous Normalizing Flows that regresses straight-line vector fields between noise and data, enabling faster sampling
Matching flow rates in computer cooling systems
A sorting algorithm for graphs
A method for packet inspection
quiz.explanation: Flow Matching provides a simulation-free training objective that learns straight probability flow trajectories, achieving high-fidelity generation in very few steps (Stable Diffusion 3, Flux).

quiz.question: What is Score-Based Generative Modeling (Song & Ermon, 2019)?
options: Estimating the score function (the gradient of the log data density with respect to input: grad_x log p(x)) and sampling via Langevin dynamics
Grading models with an exam score
A model that predicts sports scores
A benchmark for image classifiers
quiz.explanation: Score-based modeling learns vector fields pointing toward regions of high probability density, integrating seamlessly with continuous stochastic differential equations (SDEs).

quiz.question: What is Fréchet Inception Distance (FID)?
options: The gold-standard metric for evaluating generative image quality and diversity by comparing feature statistics of real and fake images from an Inception-v3 network
The physical distance between GPUs in meters
The training time of a GAN
The percentage of duplicate images
quiz.explanation: FID measures the Wasserstein-2 distance between multivariate Gaussian approximations of Inception features: lower FID indicates superior fidelity and realism.

quiz.question: What does Inception Score (IS) measure in generative models?
options: Both the sharpness/clarity of generated images (low entropy conditional distribution P(y|x)) and diversity across classes (high entropy marginal distribution P(y))
The speed of the Inception network
The number of layers in Inception-v3
The GPU clock frequency
quiz.explanation: Inception score evaluates whether individual samples clearly belong to specific classes while ensuring the overall generated set covers all classes diversely.

quiz.question: What is Image-to-Image (img2img) translation in diffusion models?
options: Adding partial noise to an existing input image (e.g. to step t=500 of 1000) and running reverse diffusion from that midpoint conditioned on a new text prompt
Converting PNG files to JPEG
Upscaling images with bilinear interpolation
Inverting colors of an image
quiz.explanation: Img2img preserves the high-level structural composition of the input image while regenerating stylistic textures guided by the conditioning prompt.

quiz.question: What is Inpainting in generative computer vision?
options: Synthesizing realistic image content to seamlessly fill in a user-masked missing or erased region of an image conditioned on surrounding context
Painting physical canvases with robots
Colorizing black and white photos only
Removing all background pixels
quiz.explanation: Inpainting replaces masked areas with contextually coherent content while holding the unmasked boundaries fixed.

quiz.question: What is ControlNet (Zhang et al., 2023)?
options: An architectural adapter that locks a pretrained diffusion model and adds trainable task-specific conditioning (edges, poses, depth maps) via zero-convolutions
A controller for smart home devices
An internet networking protocol
A tool for controlling GPU temperatures
quiz.explanation: ControlNet adds spatial conditioning controls (such as Canny edge maps, OpenPose human skeletons, or depth maps) to text-to-image models with remarkable spatial precision.

quiz.question: What is DreamBooth (Ruiz et al., Google 2022)?
options: Fine-tuning a diffusion model on 3-5 images of a specific subject bound to a unique rare token identifier (e.g. 'a [V] dog') with class-specific prior preservation loss
A photobooth app for smartphones
A tool for generating lucid dreams
A video conferencing background tool
quiz.explanation: DreamBooth personalizes text-to-image models to synthesize novel scenes containing a specific person, pet, or custom object while maintaining identity consistency.

quiz.question: What is Textual Inversion (Gal et al., 2022)?
options: Learning a single new pseudo-word embedding vector in a frozen text encoder's vocabulary to represent a custom concept without modifying any model weights
Inverting text strings backwards
Translating text into binary code
Inverting attention weights
quiz.explanation: Textual Inversion freezes the entire diffusion model and optimizes only a single 768-dim token embedding that captures the visual concept.

quiz.question: What is Consistency Model (Song et al., OpenAI 2023)?
options: A generative model that maps any point along a diffusion trajectory directly to the origin data point, enabling high-quality generation in a single sampling step
A model that never contradicts itself
A database consistency check
A rule-based reasoning engine
quiz.explanation: Consistency models enforce self-consistency along probability flow trajectories, allowing 1-step or 2-step image generation without iterative ODE integration.
